title: Synthetic Imagination II: An exploration of composition
author: @sfiscience
text:
Luigi Russolo and Ugo Piatti (Italian Futurists) in their Milanese intonarumori workshop, ca. 1916November 3, 2026This past September, SFI Director of Experimental Projects, Caitlin McShea, and SFI Research Fellow Tony Eagan co-hosted the Santa Fe Institute’s second annual Synthetic Imagination event, a multi-day symposium exploring human innovation. 

Last year’s inaugural session was devoted to the role imagination plays in architecture and urban design. This year was devoted to composition. Eagan and McShea aimed to weave together talks and performances with deep and delicate connections enough to make the event itself a model of human composition. 

Musician Canton Becker, who moderated a panel that included SFI Professor Melanie Mitchell and External Professor Marco Buongiorno Nardelli (University of North Texas), reflected after the event, “SFI’s ‘Synthetic Imagination’ reminded me of what synthesis originally meant: to bring disparate elements together into a new whole. The symposium exemplified this definition. Neuroscience, music, cuisine, artificial intelligence, puzzles, theater, and films were curated in such a way that they became a single conversation.”

While much of “Synthetic Imagination” was restricted to a small, invited audience at SFI’s Gurley Forum, the event was bookended by public events held at Santa Fe’s Center for Contemporary Arts. Presentations began on Tuesday evening with a screening of Leonora in the Morning Light, a biographical drama about the surrealist painter and novelist, Leonora Carrington, followed by a panel discussion with SFI President David Krakauer and film directors Thor Klein and Lena Vurma.

The program concluded on Saturday with Opus Cope: An Algorithmic Opera, a documentary about David Cope, who created Experiments in Musical Intelligence (EMI). EMI was an early algorithmic system that generated music in the style of different historical composers. Jae Shim, who wrote, directed, filmed, and edited the documentary, was on hand to discuss the gray areas between the fruits of human creativity and those of artificial intelligence. 

The intervening days included talks from SFI Professor Cris Moore on how to construct beguiling puzzles; James Beard Award nominee Christian Pontiggia on composing culinary delights; neurobiologist Leslie Kay on the “multi-sensory dynamics of flavor”; and Tony Eagan on William Basinski’s decomposing music. 

Zen leader and poet Henry Shukman gave a talk on how poetry allows one to relive the past and thus experience it for the first time, while educator, author, and musician Peter Pesic concluded the presentations with a piano concert entitled “Mimesis and Creation,” during which he performed pieces by Olivier Messiaen, Maurice Ravel, and Claude Debussy. 

On day two, playwright Matthew Libby spoke on the craft of constructing work for theater. Following his talk, actors Jihan Haddad and Madeleine Barker performed a moving stage reading of Libby’s play Sisters, the 2022 Neukom Institute Literary Arts Award winner about a lifelong relationship between a young woman and her AI sibling. 

During last year’s event, the organizers proposed that the imagination may be the faculty that most distinguishes humans from so-called alien intelligences (AI included). This year, questions around this idea were all the more pressing, given the advances we have seen among AI technologies. Together, the speakers and spectators pursued the question of how much the ontological status — that is, living, dead, human, machine — matters to an audience, and just where we can draw the line between the human ability to synthesize, editorialize, and judge, and the ability of “synthetic” operators in these same tasks.

Remarking on the meeting after it concluded, McShea said, “Each artist strives to communicate a place in this world with some compositional choice — a pentomino, a profane line of dialogue, a reflection, a mushroom mousse, an emphasis placed upon a certain chord, a moment in time.” Synthetic Imagination II: An exploration of compositionAgent-Based Modeling: Worlds Within WorldsBuilding better digital twinsProofs and reasons: How math works in the mindA review of "The Traveler"Of midterms, mayors, and complex political identityRandom walks get pushyThe complexity of scientific optimism: A review of "It Could Be Otherwise"Change the number of searchers, change the efficiency of a questModeling social inequality in epidemicsSFI welcomes 2026 External ProfessorsImplicit biases are harder to change in big cities than in small citiesNew study examines publication trends at top journalsCoordinating international operations with “Space Diplomacy”Multiroute Pathogen Transmission is DifferentAllison Stanger named a 2026–27 Berlin Prize FellowIn Memoriam: Peter SchusterCooperation both protects and weakens societiesKaleda Denton selected as a “Rising Star in Computational and Data Sciences”Andreas Wagner awarded ERC Advanced Grant
